claim: Individuals vary markedly in their avoidance of detrimental consequences, that is in their sensitivity to punishment.
source: It has been reported that individuals vary markedly in their avoidance of detrimental consequences, that is in their sensitivity to punishment.
evidence: This is stated as a reported finding in the abstract, drawing on established literature.

claim: Punishment insensitivity is a unique phenotype, unrelated to differences in reward-seeking and Pavlovian fear.
source: We show that punishment insensitivity is a unique phenotype, unrelated to differences in reward-seeking and Pavlovian fear, and due to a failure of instrumental control.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Punishment insensitivity is due to a failure of instrumental control.
source: We show that punishment insensitivity is a unique phenotype, unrelated to differences in reward-seeking and Pavlovian fear, and due to a failure of instrumental control.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and analysis.

claim: Subjects insensitive to punishment are afraid of aversive events but unable to change their behaviour to avoid them.
source: Subjects insensitive to punishment are afraid of aversive events, they are simply unable to change their behaviour to avoid them.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing intact fear responses but impaired punishment learning.

claim: Reward and punishment are among the most fundamental psychological building blocks of behaviour.
source: Reward and punishment are among the most fundamental psychological building blocks of behaviour.
evidence: This is a statement drawing on established scientific consensus in psychology and behavioral science.

claim: Punishment sensitivity plays an important role in normal learning, decision making as well as emotion.
source: Punishment sensitivity plays an important role in normal learning, decision making as well as emotion (Corr, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Corr, 2004.

claim: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of conduct disorder.
source: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of a range of psychopathologies including conduct disorder (Briggs-Gowan et al., 2014; Dadds and Salmon, 2003), drug and behavioural addictions (Vanderschuren et al., 2017), eating disorders (Monteleone et al., 2018), psychopathy (Blair et al., 2006; Gregory et al., 2015), and depression (Elliott et al., 1996; Eshel and Roiser, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Briggs-Gowan et al., 2014 and Dadds and Salmon, 2003.

claim: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of drug and behavioural addictions.
source: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of a range of psychopathologies including conduct disorder (Briggs-Gowan et al., 2014; Dadds and Salmon, 2003), drug and behavioural addictions (Vanderschuren et al., 2017), eating disorders (Monteleone et al., 2018), psychopathy (Blair et al., 2006; Gregory et al., 2015), and depression (Elliott et al., 1996; Eshel and Roiser, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vanderschuren et al., 2017.

claim: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of eating disorders.
source: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of a range of psychopathologies including conduct disorder (Briggs-Gowan et al., 2014; Dadds and Salmon, 2003), drug and behavioural addictions (Vanderschuren et al., 2017), eating disorders (Monteleone et al., 2018), psychopathy (Blair et al., 2006; Gregory et al., 2015), and depression (Elliott et al., 1996; Eshel and Roiser, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Monteleone et al., 2018.

claim: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of psychopathy.
source: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of a range of psychopathologies including conduct disorder (Briggs-Gowan et al., 2014; Dadds and Salmon, 2003), drug and behavioural addictions (Vanderschuren et al., 2017), eating disorders (Monteleone et al., 2018), psychopathy (Blair et al., 2006; Gregory et al., 2015), and depression (Elliott et al., 1996; Eshel and Roiser, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blair et al., 2006 and Gregory et al., 2015.

claim: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of depression.
source: Differences in sensitivity to punishment have been implicated in the aetiology or maintenance of a range of psychopathologies including conduct disorder (Briggs-Gowan et al., 2014; Dadds and Salmon, 2003), drug and behavioural addictions (Vanderschuren et al., 2017), eating disorders (Monteleone et al., 2018), psychopathy (Blair et al., 2006; Gregory et al., 2015), and depression (Elliott et al., 1996; Eshel and Roiser, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Elliott et al., 1996 and Eshel and Roiser, 2010.

claim: Punishment sensitivity is an increasingly popular measure of the motivation to engage in drug-seeking and drug-taking.
source: Moreover, punishment sensitivity is an increasingly popular measure of the motivation to engage in drug-seeking and drug-taking (Augier et al., 2018; Deroche-Gamonet et al., 2004; Kasanetz et al., 2013; Marchant et al., 2018; Pascoli et al., 2015; Vanderschuren and Everitt, 2004; Vanderschuren et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Individual differences in punishment learning may be due to temperamental differences in aversive valuation or aversion sensitivity.
source: First, individual differences in punishment learning may be due to temperamental differences in aversive valuation or aversion sensitivity (Corr, 2004; Gray, 1970).
evidence: This is a hypothesis presented in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Punishment insensitive individuals may show reward dominance, with choices and behaviour more strongly determined via the value of any rewards they earn rather than any punishment they incur.
source: A second possibility is that punishment insensitive individuals show reward dominance, with choices and behaviour more strongly determined via the value of any rewards they earn rather than any punishment they incur (O'Brien and Frick, 1996; Robinson and Berridge, 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis presented in the introduction, supported by citations.

claim: Individual differences in punishment sensitivity may emerge from individual differences in aversive instrumental learning and control.
source: A final, and not mutually exclusive, possibility is that individual differences in punishment sensitivity emerge from individual differences in aversive instrumental learning and control (Seligman, 1970).
evidence: This is a hypothesis presented in the introduction, supported by a citation.

claim: The magnitude of the unconditioned response to a stimulus has little bearing on what is learned about that stimulus.
source: However, the magnitude of the unconditioned response to a stimulus has little bearing on what is learned about that stimulus (Rescorla, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rescorla, 1988.

claim: Prior to aversive training, there was no preference between pressing the to-be-punished versus unpunished lever.
source: Prior to aversive training, there was no preference between pressing the to-be-punished versus unpunished lever (F(1,47) = .071; p = 0.791, ηp2 0.001) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 2.

claim: There was less lever pressing on the punished lever than the unpunished lever during aversive training.
source: There was evidence for punishment learning because there was less lever pressing on the punished lever than the unpunished lever (the traditional measure of punishment learning in this task) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Punishment avoidance increased across days of training.
source: Punishment avoidance increased across days (linear trend: F (1,47)=7.49; p=0.009, ηp2 0.137).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Significant punishment suppression was observed for each session of aversive training.
source: Follow-up analyses revealed significant punishment suppression for each session (1st session: F (1,47)=5.48; p=0.024, ηp2 0.137; remaining sessions: F (1,47)>23.4; p<0.001, ηp2 0.332).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Conditioned suppression elicited by presentations of the CS+ increased across training.
source: Conditioned suppression elicited by presentations of the CS+ also increased across training (F (1,47)=35.1; p<0.001, ηp2 0.427), with significant suppression being observed for each session (all F (1,47)>54.7; p<0.001, ηp2 0.537).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Punishment suppression appeared to be bimodally distributed with some subjects showing strong punishment sensitivity and others weaker or no punishment suppression.
source: Punishment suppression appeared to be bimodally distributed with some subjects showing strong punishment suppression (i.e. punishment sensitivity) and others weaker or no punishment suppression (i.e. punishment insensitivity) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was variation in Pavlovian fear among subjects, albeit less pronounced than variation in punishment suppression.
source: There was also, albeit less pronounced, variation in Pavlovian fear (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At the group level, there was a main effect of lever on suppression ratios.
source: At the group level, this analysis showed a main effect of lever (F(1,47) = 44.39; p<0.001, ηp2 0.485), session (linear: F(1,47) = 9.476; p=0.003, ηp2 0.167), and a significant lever x session interaction (F(1,47) = 10.62; p=0.002, ηp2 0.184).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The lever x session interaction was driven by a significant increase in the unpunished suppression ratio across sessions.
source: This interaction was driven by a significant increase in the unpunished suppression ratio across sessions (linear: F(1,47) = 24.54; p<0.001, ηp2 0.343), but no significant change in punished lever suppression (linear: F(1,47) = .210; p = 0.649, ηp2 0.004).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Punished lever suppression was significantly greater than unpunished lever suppression for all sessions.
source: Punished lever suppression was significantly greater than unpunished lever suppression for all sessions (F(1,47) > 9.22; p<0.004, ηp2 0.164).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Suppression of responding on the punished lever, but not the unpunished lever, appeared bimodal at the individual subject level.
source: Examination of individual subject performances showed that suppression of responding on the punished lever, but not the unpunished lever, appeared bimodal (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Strong positive correlations were observed among each measure (punishment, fear, reward) across sessions.
source: We observed strong positive correlations among each of these measures across sessions, showing that each subject's relative behaviour was stable across days.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Few significant positive correlations were observed between the measures of punishment, fear, and reward.
source: However, we observed few significant positive correlations between the measures.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For fear and punishment, the only significant correlation was negative and present only on the first day of training.
source: Notably, for fear and punishment, the only significant correlation was negative and present only on the first day of training.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Multidimensional scaling showed that punishment, fear, and reward clustered in separate spaces.
source: This showed that punishment, fear, and reward clustered in separate spaces.
evidence: This is supported by multidimensional scaling analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Punished lever suppression was clustered in a separate space from conditioned suppression, suggesting that punishment and fear are highly dissimilar to each other.
source: Punished lever suppression was clustered in a separate space from conditioned suppression, suggesting that punishment and fear are highly dissimilar to each other.
evidence: This is an inference from the multidimensional scaling analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Unpunished lever suppression was initially closely related to punished response suppression but became progressively different as training progressed.
source: Unpunished lever suppression was initially closely related to punished response suppression but became progressively different as training progressed.
evidence: This is an observation from the multidimensional scaling analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A 4-component solution was optimal in Principal Components Analysis, accounting for 75.9% of overall variance.
source: A 4-component solution was optimal, accounting for 75.9% of overall variance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), with most measures well captured by these four components (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The first component in PCA captured the influence of punishment, with punishment suppression across training loading strongly on this component.
source: The first component captured the influence of punishment: punishment suppression across the course of training loaded strongly on this component.
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The second component in PCA captured the influence of contextual fear learning early during training.
source: The second component captured the influence of contextual fear learning early during training: both initial punishment suppression and unpunished responding loaded positively on this component whereas CS+ suppression loaded negatively.
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The third component in PCA captured specific CS+ fear from later in training.
source: The third component captured specific CS+ fear from later in training: only CS+ suppression loaded positively on this component.
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The fourth component in PCA captured reward.
source: The fourth component captured reward: the remainder of the variance in unpunished responding loaded positively on this component.
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Punishment and fear do not load positively on the same component in PCA.
source: So, punishment and fear do not load positively on the same component.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Any relationship between punishment and fear was largely negative, indicative of a competitive rather than complementary relationship.
source: In fact, any relationship between them was largely negative, indicative of a competitive rather than complementary relationship between them.
evidence: This is an inference from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Factor Analysis results were similar to PCA.
source: The results from this analysis were similar to PCA (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of FA and PCA results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Variation in aversive learning can be accounted for by an influence of punishment (Factor 1), contextual fear (Factor 2), CS+ fear (Factor 3), and reward (Factor 4).
source: Based on factor loadings, variation in aversive learning can be accounted for by an influence of punishment (Factor 1), contextual fear (Factor 2), CS+ fear (Factor 3), and reward (Factor 4).
evidence: This is supported by Factor Analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Punishment, reward, and fear are largely orthogonal to each other.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest punishment, reward, and fear are largely orthogonal each other.
evidence: This is a conclusion from PCA and FA analyses shown in Figure 5.

claim: Training lever-pressing was correlated with unpunished but not punished lever-press rates during ITIs.
source: Training lever-pressing was correlated with unpunished (average r = 0.561, p<0.0001) but not punished lever-press rates during ITIs (average r = 0.198, p=0.18) or conditioned suppression (average r = 0.173, p=0.24).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Responding during training predicts later unpunished responding but not punishment or conditioned suppression.
source: This implies responding during training predicts later unpunished responding but not punishment or conditioned suppression.
evidence: This is an inference from correlation analysis and PCA shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lever-press suppression ratios were not correlated with training lever-press rate.
source: Lever-press suppression ratios, which remove variability attributable to pre-punishment differences in reward-seeking, were not correlated with training lever-press rate (punished lever suppression: r = −0.06, p=0.69; unpunished lever suppression: r = −0.04, p=0.79), again indicating that punishment-driven changes in lever-pressing are unrelated to initial rates of lever pressing.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Silhouette values revealed positive silhouette values for 2–4 k-mean clusters.
source: Silhouette values revealed positive silhouette values for 2–4 k-mean clusters, which were each marginally higher compared to solutions using more clusters.
evidence: This is supported by cluster analysis.

claim: The groups produced by the 2-cluster solution did not differ in sex.
source: The groups produced by the 2-cluster solution did not differ in sex (χ2(1)=0.782, p=0.376; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two clusters from the 2-cluster solution did not differ in pre-punishment lever-pressing.
source: The two clusters did not differ in pre-punishment lever-pressing (all F(1,46) ≤. 659, p ≥. 421; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), showing that they did not differ in reward learning prior to aversive learning.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two clusters from the 2-cluster solution were distinguishable by their punishment avoidance.
source: They were, however, distinguishable by their punishment avoidance, regardless of whether this was measured via punished lever suppression or preference ratio (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significant overall difference in punished lever suppression between clusters across sessions in the 2-cluster solution.
source: Specifically, there was a significant overall difference in punished lever suppression (F(1,46) = 105.96, p<0.001, ηp2 0.697) (Figure 6A) and preference ratio (F(1,46) = 49.13, p<0.001, ηp2 0.517) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) between clusters across sessions.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was no main effect of cluster on unpunished lever suppression in the 2-cluster solution.
source: However, there was no main effect of cluster on either unpunished lever suppression (F(1,46) = .215, p = 0.645) (Figure 6A) or conditioned suppression (F(1,46) = 1.008, p=0.321, ηp2 0.021) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was no main effect of cluster on conditioned suppression in the 2-cluster solution.
source: However, there was no main effect of cluster on either unpunished lever suppression (F(1,46) = .215, p = 0.645) (Figure 6A) or conditioned suppression (F(1,46) = 1.008, p=0.321, ηp2 0.021) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The punishment-sensitive group significantly suppressed punished but not unpunished responding relative to pre-punishment.
source: Further analyses showed that the punishment-sensitive group significantly suppressed punished (F(1,46) = 333.638, p<0.001, ηp2 0.878) but not unpunished (F(1,46) = 2.601, p=0.114, ηp2 0.053) responding relative to pre-punishment.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The punishment-insensitive group modestly suppressed both punished and unpunished responding relative to pre-punishment.
source: In contrast, the punishment-insensitive group modestly suppressed both punished (F(1,46) = 75.318, p<0.001, ηp2 0.621) and unpunished (F(1,46) = 10.395, p=0.002, ηp2 0.184) responding relative to pre-punishment.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The punishment-insensitive group were not simply showing attenuated punishment but were instead showing a distinct suppression phenotype.
source: This shows that the punishment-insensitive group were not simply showing attenuated punishment but were instead showing a distinct suppression phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analysis of the 2-cluster solution.

claim: Shock intensities for the punishment-insensitive cluster had been increased more than for punishment-sensitive cluster.
source: Due to this differential ITI suppression across groups, shock intensities for the punishment-insensitive cluster had been increased more than for punishment-sensitive cluster (linear x cluster interaction: F(1,46) = 6.062, p=0.018; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), although shock intensity did not differ overall across sessions (F(1,45) = 2.196, p=0.145).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Shock intensity was not a significant covariate for final punishment or conditioned suppression in the 2-cluster solution.
source: Importantly, shock intensity was not a significant covariate for final punishment (F(1,45) = 1.042, p=0.313) or conditioned suppression (F(1,45) = .389, p = 0.536), showing this was not a driving factor for cluster differences.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A significant effect of sex was found in the 3-cluster solution.
source: When a 3-cluster solution was derived, a significant effect of sex was found (χ2 (2)=7.416, p=0.025; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hyper-sensitive cluster exhibited initial indiscriminate suppression on both the punished and unpunished levers.
source: The last cluster (half-filled symbols; n = 4 [4 female]; Figure 7C) was a small cohort that exhibited initial indiscriminate suppression on both the punished and unpunished levers as well as a counterintuitive increase in pressing during the CS+ during initial sessions.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The hyper-sensitive cluster exhibited a counterintuitive increase in pressing during the CS+ during initial sessions.
source: The last cluster (half-filled symbols; n = 4 [4 female]; Figure 7C) was a small cohort that exhibited initial indiscriminate suppression on both the punished and unpunished levers as well as a counterintuitive increase in pressing during the CS+ during initial sessions.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In later sessions, the hyper-sensitive cluster exhibited the greatest conditioned and punished lever suppression.
source: However, in later sessions, this cluster exhibited the greatest conditioned and punished lever suppression.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The clusters in the 3-cluster solution did not differ in lever-press rates across training.
source: Once again, the clusters did not differ in lever-press rates across training (all F(2,45) ≤ 1.886, p ≥. 164; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: All clusters in the 3-cluster solution showed significant punished lever suppression averaged across punishment.
source: Compared to pre-punishment lever-pressing, all clusters showed significant punished lever suppression averaged across punishment (F(1,45) ≥ 45.374, p<0.001, ηp2 0.502) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The punishment-insensitive cluster showed the least punished lever suppression in the 3-cluster solution.
source: Specifically, the punishment-insensitive cluster showed the least (F(1,45) ≥ 66.55, p<0.001, ηp2 0.596) and the hyper-sensitive cluster showed the most F(1,45) ≥ 4.386, p ≤. 0419, ηp2 0.089) punished lever suppression.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The hyper-sensitive cluster showed the most punished lever suppression in the 3-cluster solution.
source: Specifically, the punishment-insensitive cluster showed the least (F(1,45) ≥ 66.55, p<0.001, ηp2 0.596) and the hyper-sensitive cluster showed the most F(1,45) ≥ 4.386, p ≤. 0419, ηp2 0.089) punished lever suppression.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The clusters in the 3-cluster solution differed on unpunished lever suppression relative to pre-training.
source: The clusters also differed on unpunished lever suppression relative to pre-training (F(1,45) ≥ 15.54, p<0.001, ηp2 0.257) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The punishment-sensitive cluster showed no unpunished lever suppression in the 3-cluster solution.
source: The punishment-sensitive cluster showed no (F(1,45) = 1.164, p=0.286, ηp2 0.025), the punishment-insensitive cluster showed moderate (F(1,45) = 24.828, p<0.001, ηp2 0.356), whereas the hyper-sensitive cluster showed the most suppression (F(1,45) = 61.932, p<0.001, ηp2 0.579).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The punishment-insensitive cluster showed moderate unpunished lever suppression in the 3-cluster solution.
source: The punishment-sensitive cluster showed no (F(1,45) = 1.164, p=0.286, ηp2 0.025), the punishment-insensitive cluster showed moderate (F(1,45) = 24.828, p<0.001, ηp2 0.356), whereas the hyper-sensitive cluster showed the most suppression (F(1,45) = 61.932, p<0.001, ηp2 0.579).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The hyper-sensitive cluster showed the most unpunished lever suppression in the 3-cluster solution.
source: The punishment-sensitive cluster showed no (F(1,45) = 1.164, p=0.286, ηp2 0.025), the punishment-insensitive cluster showed moderate (F(1,45) = 24.828, p<0.001, ηp2 0.356), whereas the hyper-sensitive cluster showed the most suppression (F(1,45) = 61.932, p<0.001, ηp2 0.579).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Both the punishment-sensitive and hyper-sensitive clusters increasingly differentiated between punished and unpunished lever suppression across sessions.
source: Both the punishment-sensitive (F(1,45) = 13.84, p<0.001, ηp2 0.235) and hyper-sensitive clusters (F(1,45) = 20.471, p<0.001, ηp2 0.137) increasingly differentiated between punished and unpunished lever suppression across sessions whereas the punishment-insensitive cluster did not (F(1,45) = .168, p = 0.684).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The punishment-insensitive cluster did not increasingly differentiate between punished and unpunished lever suppression across sessions.
source: Both the punishment-sensitive (F(1,45) = 13.84, p<0.001, ηp2 0.235) and hyper-sensitive clusters (F(1,45) = 20.471, p<0.001, ηp2 0.137) increasingly differentiated between punished and unpunished lever suppression across sessions whereas the punishment-insensitive cluster did not (F(1,45) = .168, p = 0.684).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The punishment-sensitive cluster exhibited differential suppression for all sessions in the 3-cluster solution.
source: The punishment-sensitive cluster exhibited differential suppression for all sessions (F(1,45) ≥ 18.585, p < 0.001, ηp2 0.292), whereas the hyper-sensitive cluster only showed significantly different lever suppression from session four onwards (F(1,45) ≥ 15.088, p<0.001, ηp2 0.251).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The hyper-sensitive cluster only showed significantly different lever suppression from session four onwards.
source: The punishment-sensitive cluster exhibited differential suppression for all sessions (F(1,45) ≥ 18.585, p < 0.001, ηp2 0.292), whereas the hyper-sensitive cluster only showed significantly different lever suppression from session four onwards (F(1,45) ≥ 15.088, p<0.001, ηp2 0.251).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The punishment-sensitive cluster initially suppressed but subsequently elevated rates of unpunished responding relative to pre-punishment training.
source: The punishment-sensitive cluster also initially suppressed (session 1–2: F(1,45) ≥ 5.934, p ≤. 019, ηp2 0.117) but subsequently elevated (session 3–6: F(1,45) ≥ 4.129, p ≤. 048) rates of unpunished responding relative to pre-punishment training.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The hyper-sensitive cluster drastically suppressed unpunished responding early during aversive training, but this recovered and they eventually pressed at rates equivalent to pre-punishment training.
source: The hyper-sensitive cluster drastically suppressed unpunished responding early during aversive training (session 1–4: F(1,45) ≥ 19.060, p<0.001, ηp2 0.298), but this recovered and they eventually pressed at rates equivalent to pre-punishment training (session 5–6: F(1,45) ≤. 070, p ≥. 793).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: All clusters in the 3-cluster solution showed greater CS+ fear across sessions.
source: All clusters showed greater CS+ fear across sessions (F(1,45) ≥ 6.08, p ≤ . 018) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7.

claim: There were no significant differences between punishment-sensitive and punishment-insensitive clusters in their conditioned suppression.
source: There were no significant differences between punishment-sensitive and punishment-insensitive clusters in their conditioned suppression (overall: F(1,45) = .517, p = 0.476, ηp2 0.011; linear: F(1,45) = .048, p = 0.828).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The hyper-sensitive cluster had a significantly greater decrease in conditioned suppression across sessions than the other clusters.
source: However, the hyper-sensitive cluster had a significantly greater decrease in conditioned suppression across sessions than the other clusters (F(1,45) ≥ 41.255, p<0.001, ηp2 0.478).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The clusters in the 3-cluster solution differed in shock increments across training.
source: The clusters differed in shock increments across training (linear x cluster interaction: F(2,45) = 6.850, p=0.003; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Shock intensity was not a significant covariate for final punishment or conditioned suppression in the 3-cluster solution.
source: However, shock intensity was not a significant covariate for final punishment (F(1,44) = 1.691, p=0.200) or conditioned suppression (F(1,44) = .834, p = 0.366), indicating that differences in shock intensity were not a driving factor for group differences.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Individual differences in punishment sensitivity cannot be predicted or explained by individual differences in fear or reward.
source: Using data-driven analytic approaches we show that these individual differences in punishment sensitivity cannot be predicted or explained by individual differences in fear or reward.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study, supported by multiple analyses (correlations, PCA, FA, MDS, clustering).

claim: Punishment, fear and reward were remarkably independent across each analysis.
source: Rather, across each analysis, punishment, fear and reward were remarkably independent.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study, supported by multiple analyses.

claim: There was no evidence to support the possibility that punishment insensitivity is due to reduced aversion sensitivity or reward dominance.
source: There was no evidence here to support the possibility that punishment insensitivity is due to reduced aversion sensitivity or reward dominance.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study, supported by the independence of punishment, fear, and reward measures.

claim: Punishment insensitivity was a failure of instrumental learning.
source: Instead, punishment insensitivity was a failure of instrumental learning.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study, supported by cluster analysis showing distinct behavioral profiles.

claim: Punishment insensitivity is most likely due to a failure to encode the instrumental response-punisher association relative to the other associations in the task.
source: It could have multiple origins but is most likely due to a failure to encode the instrumental response-punisher association relative to the other associations in the task.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study, based on the pattern of results from cluster analysis.

claim: Punishment-sensitive subjects parsed multiple contingencies to show Pavlovian and instrumental behavioral control whereas insensitive subjects were impaired in partitioning these different contingencies.
source: Our task involved multiple instrumental (response-outcome) and Pavlovian (stimulus-outcome) contingencies; punishment-sensitive subjects parsed these contingencies to show Pavlovian and instrumental behavioral control whereas insensitive subjects were impaired in partitioning these different contingencies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, based on the pattern of results from cluster analysis.

claim: Punishment-insensitive subjects exhibited modest suppression of both punished and unpunished responding, which is incompatible with the reward dominance account.
source: Punishment-insensitive subjects identified by cluster analysis exhibited modest suppression of both punished and unpunished responding. This profile of generalised behavioural suppression is incompatible with the reward dominance account, and is similar to the behaviour shown by subjects receiving response-independent aversive events (Hunt and Brady, 1951; Jean-Richard-Dit-Bressel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, based on cluster analysis and comparison to previous literature.

claim: Punishment-insensitive animals behaved as though they were not causing the aversive events they were experiencing and instead expressed weak but generalised Pavlovian fear.
source: That is, punishment-insensitive animals behaved as though they were not causing the aversive events they were experiencing and instead expressed weak but generalised Pavlovian fear.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cluster analysis results.

claim: Punishment-insensitive subjects showed intact behavioural inhibition during Pavlovian fear.
source: However, any such failure of inhibition must have been specific to the punished response and not a failure of behavioural inhibition more generally (Gray, 1982; Gray and McNaughton, 2000) because punishment-insensitive subjects showed intact behavioural inhibition during Pavlovian fear.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, based on the observation that punishment-insensitive subjects showed normal conditioned suppression.

claim: Punishment-insensitive rats were a relatively large proportion of the sample.
source: It is worth noting that punishment-insensitive rats were a relatively large proportion of the sample.
evidence: This is an observation from the cluster analysis results.

claim: The relatively lean punishment contingency applied (VI60 sec CS+) was likely a key factor in determining the number of insensitive subjects.
source: Given the evidence that impaired punishment contingency detection underpinned punishment insensitivity, it is likely the relatively lean punishment contingency applied here (VI60 sec CS+) was a key factor in determining the number of insensitive subjects.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings and design.

claim: Drugs of abuse may promote punishment resistance by impairing punishment contingency detection.
source: An intriguing possibility is that drugs of abuse may promote punishment resistance by impairing punishment contingency detection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study's findings and previous literature.

claim: Insensitivity to punishment might be reduced at high shock intensities or after extended punishment training.
source: This is consistent with demonstrations that insensitivity to punishment might be reduced at high shock intensities (Golden et al., 2017) or after extended punishment training (Cooper et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Golden et al., 2017 and Cooper et al., 2007.

claim: There was an absence of any notable co-variance between instrumental and Pavlovian aversive learning.
source: From a theoretical perspective, perhaps the most surprising finding here was the absence of any notable co-variance between instrumental and Pavlovian aversive learning, even when more powerful methods capable of detecting such underlying relationships were applied (e.g. PCA and FA).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by multiple analyses.

claim: Theories of associative learning and motivation have historically assumed that instrumental and Pavlovian determinants of behaviour share a common basis.
source: Historically, theories of associative learning and motivation have assumed that instrumental and Pavlovian determinants of behaviour share a common basis and that reinforcers have common motivational value that underpins these different forms of learning (Mackintosh, 1983; Rescorla and Solomon, 1967).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mackintosh, 1983 and Rescorla and Solomon, 1967.

claim: Distinct processes govern instrumental versus Pavlovian reward value.
source: However, it is now well understood that distinct processes govern instrumental versus Pavlovian reward value (Balleine and Dickinson, 1998; Dickinson and Balleine, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Balleine and Dickinson, 1998 and Dickinson and Balleine, 2002.

claim: The findings extend the dissociation between instrumental and Pavlovian processes to aversive learning.
source: Our findings extend this dissociation to aversive learning (see also Giuliano et al., 2018; Pelloux et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, supported by the data and citations to related work.

claim: If there is any trans-contingency encoding of outcome value, then this contributes little to how animals learn punishment and fear.
source: We show that if there is any trans-contingency encoding of outcome value, then this contributes little to how animals learn punishment and fear.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, based on the independence of punishment and fear measures.

claim: The motivational underpinnings of Pavlovian fear and punishment are distinct.
source: These two forms of aversive learning were independent of each other suggesting that the motivational underpinnings of Pavlovian fear and punishment are distinct.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, based on the independence of punishment and fear measures.

claim: Punishment tasks are widely used to model the adverse consequences of drug seeking and measure motivation to engage in drug-seeking in the face of adverse consequences.
source: Punishment tasks are widely used to model the adverse consequences of drug seeking and measure motivation to engage in drug-seeking in the face of adverse consequences (Augier et al., 2018; Kasanetz et al., 2013; Pascoli et al., 2015; Vanderschuren and Everitt, 2004; Vanderschuren et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The persistence of drug-seeking in the face of punishment is invoked as an objective behavioural marker of addiction.
source: The persistence of drug-seeking in the face of punishment (i.e. insensitivity to punishment) is invoked as an objective behavioural marker of addiction (Deroche-Gamonet et al., 2004; Vanderschuren and Everitt, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deroche-Gamonet et al., 2004 and Vanderschuren and Everitt, 2004.

claim: Insensitivity to punishment is typically attributed to drug-induced plasticity promoting reward dominance or impulsivity.
source: This insensitivity is typically attributed to drug-induced plasticity promoting reward dominance or impulsivity.
evidence: This is a statement about common interpretations in the field.

claim: Insensitivity is a characteristic of punishment itself, not solely a result of drug-induced plasticity.
source: However, a key finding here is that insensitivity is a characteristic of punishment itself.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study.

claim: Punishment insensitivity can emerge from a specific deficit in instrumental aversive learning and can be observed in studies using non-drug rewards.
source: Punishment insensitivity can emerge from a specific deficit in instrumental aversive learning and can be observed in studies using non-drug rewards.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study.

claim: Punishment insensitivity can pre-exist any drug-induced plasticity promoting reward dominance or impulsivity.
source: This suggests that punishment insensitivity can pre-exist any drug-induced plasticity promoting reward dominance or impulsivity and this pre-existing difference may provide one basis for persistence of reward seeking in the face of punishment.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study with implications for understanding addiction.

claim: Increased sensitivity to punishment is characteristic of depressive disorders.
source: Increased sensitivity to punishment is characteristic of depressive disorders; these individuals show catastrophic, globalised reactions to punishment (Elliott et al., 1996; Eshel and Roiser, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Elliott et al., 1996 and Eshel and Roiser, 2010.

claim: Cluster analyses identified a hyper-sensitive phenotype that initially displayed pronounced and indiscriminate suppression of behaviour.
source: Cluster analyses here identified a hyper-sensitive phenotype that initially displayed pronounced and indiscriminate suppression of behaviour, commensurate with pronounced Pavlovian fear, before showing exaggerated punishment and appropriate discrimination between punished and unpunished behaviour.
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis.

claim: The transition from fear to punishment among hypersensitive animals was rapid and occurred within two sessions.
source: The transition from fear to punishment among hypersensitive animals was rapid and occurred within two sessions.
evidence: This is an observation from the cluster analysis of the hyper-sensitive group.

claim: There were no sex differences among the sensitive and insensitive phenotypes.
source: Moreover, although there were no sex differences among the sensitive and insensitive phenotypes, the hypersensitive cluster was comprised exclusively of females.
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis.

claim: The hypersensitive cluster was comprised exclusively of females.
source: Moreover, although there were no sex differences among the sensitive and insensitive phenotypes, the hypersensitive cluster was comprised exclusively of females.
evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis.

claim: Subjects were 48 experimentally naive adult male and female Long-Evans rats (18 females).
source: Subjects were experimentally naive adult male and female Long-Evans rats (N = 48, 18 females) supplied by the University of New South Wales (Sydney, NSW, Australia).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The group size was chosen based on past research suggesting it would be sufficient to identify individual differences in punishment.
source: This group size was chosen based on past research (Marchant et al., 2018) suggesting that it would be sufficient to identify individual differences in punishment.
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by a citation.

claim: Animals were food restricted to maintain them at ~90% of free-feeding weight.
source: Animals were food restricted from 3 days prior to the experiment onwards (10–15 g food per day for males, 7–12 g for females) to maintain them at ~90% of free-feeding weight, with ad libitum access to water.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: All procedures were approved by the UNSW Animal Ethics Committee and in accordance with NHMRC guidelines.
source: All procedures were approved by the UNSW Animal Ethics Committee (AEC) and in accordance with the code set out by the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) for the treatment of animals in research.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: CS+ and CS- were 10 s 3 kHz tone or 5 Hz flashing light, counterbalanced.
source: CS+ and CS- were 10 s 3 kHz tone or 5 Hz flashing light, counterbalanced.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Shocks were 0.5 secs, 0.3–0.6mA.
source: Shocks (0.5 secs, 0.3–0.6mA) were delivered via the grid floor.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Rats received one session of magazine training, during which pellets were delivered on a VI-60s schedule.
source: Rats received one session of magazine training, during which pellets were delivered on a variable 60 s interval (VI-60s) schedule until 20 pellets were delivered or 30 min had elapsed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Following magazine training, rats were trained to press two levers equally on an escalating reinforcement schedule.
source: Following magazine training, rats were trained to press two levers equally on an escalating reinforcement schedule.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Following lever-press training, rats received 6 days of conditioned punishment training.
source: Following lever-press training, rats received 6 days of conditioned punishment training.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In conditioned punishment sessions, the punished lever yielded an aversive CS+ (VI-60s), while pressing the unpunished lever yielded a neutral CS- (VI-60s).
source: In these sessions, the punished lever also yielded an aversive CS+ (VI-60s), while pressing the other unpunished lever yielded a neutral CS- (VI-60s).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The CS+ co-terminated with a 0.5 s footshock.
source: The CS+ co-terminated with a 0.5 s footshock and the CS- terminated by itself.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: For the first session, footshock intensity was set at .3mA.
source: For the first session, footshock intensity was set at. 3mA.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Shock intensity was intermittently incremented by .1mA between sessions (up to .6mA) if suppression of ITI lever-pressing was not observed.
source: Shock intensity was intermittently incremented by. 1mA between sessions (up to. 6mA) if suppression of ITI lever-pressing was not observed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.
